ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the figure, there are two congruent equilateral triangles overlapping, one vertex facing upward and one vertex facing downward; the corresponding sides of the two triangles are parallel to each other. The shaded part is their intersection, forming a hexagon, with the six sides alternately lying on the boundaries of the two triangles. Reasoning: The perimeter of each equilateral triangle is 18, so the side length is s = 18/3 = 6. According to the method in the problem statement, take 60-degree oblique coordinates parallel to two groups of sides of the equilateral triangles. Let the upward triangle be U: x >= 0, y >= 0, x + y <= s. The other congruent and reversed triangle can be written as D: x <= a, y <= b, x + y >= a + b - s. The shaded region in the figure is a hexagon whose six sides are all cut out. Its six side lengths can be divided into three groups and each appears twice: s - a, s - b, a + b - s. Therefore the perimeter of the shaded hexagon is 2[(s - a) + (s - b) + (a + b - s)] = 2s = 12.

method.method_draft: Use a visual dissection of the triangle sides. From the image, label the three different directions of the shaded hexagon; opposite shaded sides are parallel and equal in the same repeating pattern, so let three consecutive shaded side lengths be a, b, and c. Around the shaded hexagon, the unshaded corner pieces cut off from the large triangles are small equilateral triangles because every angle comes from parallel sides of equilateral triangles. Looking at any one side of one large triangle in the picture, that full side is made of one shaded hexagon side plus two adjacent small equilateral-tip sides. By the parallel/equilateral congruences, those three pieces have lengths a, b, and c in some order. Therefore a + b + c equals the side length of a large triangle, which is 18/3 = 6.
